title: GIAC GWAPT
summary: The GIAC Web Application Penetration Tester certification, exam code GWAPT, is a specialist offensive security credential from GIAC, the certification body of the SANS Institute. It is aimed at penetration testers, application security engineers and developers who need to assess web applications rather than whole networks. Passing it shows an employer that you understand how a modern web application is built and how it can be attacked, including reconnaissance, authentication and session flaws, injection bugs, client side attacks and business logic weaknesses. The exam is proctored and combines multiple choice questions with performance based items, and GIAC exams allow a printed index that you prepare yourself. A pass is valid for several years and is renewed through continuing education credits. It leads to roles such as web application penetration tester, application security engineer, product security analyst or secure code reviewer. GIAC revises its outlines over time, so the domain list below follows the published outline and you should check the current version before you book. This is an independent study guide and it is not approved or sponsored by GIAC or SANS.

beginner.definition: This is a certification from GIAC about testing the security of websites and web applications. A web application is a program you use through a browser, such as an online shop or a staff portal. The exam checks that you can find weaknesses in these programs and explain how to fix them. It is meant for people who already understand how the web works.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most attacks on companies now start through a web application, so this skill is in demand. This certificate proves you can test an application properly instead of only running a scanner. It supports tester and application security roles, which sit close to development teams. It also shows that you understand the code and the design, not only the tools. For someone moving from general testing into application security, it is a clear step.
howItWorks: Learn the basics of how a browser talks to a server, including requests, responses and cookies.
Set up your own practice application in a lab that you are allowed to attack.
Study one weakness family at a time, such as injection, then test it by hand with a proxy tool.
Learn how authentication and session handling can be broken in subtle ways.
Review the client side, because attacks that run in the browser are part of the exam.
Prepare a printed index and take the official practice test before you book.
beginner.example: Imagine a staff portal where you log in with a username and a password. The login page looks safe, but the session cookie never changes after login, so anyone who steals that cookie stays logged in as you. A scanner reports nothing, because nothing is broken in an obvious way. A tester notices the flaw by watching the requests and trying a few careful steps. The exam asks for that kind of patient, hands on observation rather than a tool result, and it also asks how you would explain the risk to a developer.
takeaways: You must learn how web applications are built before you can test them well.
Hands on practice with a proxy tool matters, because the exam includes practical tasks.
Report writing counts, so practise explaining each flaw and its fix in plain language.

objectives: Describe how browsers, servers and web technologies exchange data.
Map the visible surface of a web application before testing it.
Test authentication, authorisation and session handling for weaknesses.
Find and confirm injection flaws without damaging the target.
Assess client side attacks that affect a user browser session.
Explain application logic flaws and recommend practical fixes.

chapters.title: Web application technologies and architecture
objectives: Trace a request from the browser through to the application and its database.
Explain how cookies, tokens and sessions keep a user logged in.
Recognise the common frameworks and languages used to build web applications.
Describe how a proxy sits between the browser and the server during a test.
Identify the components that make up the attack surface of a web application.

chapters.title: Reconnaissance and mapping of a web application
objectives: Enumerate directories, files and parameters that the application exposes.
Read client side code to find hidden endpoints and logic.
Identify the technologies and versions in use from their responses.
Record the application map so testing can be repeated and reported.
Decide which areas carry the highest risk and test them first.

chapters.title: Authentication, authorisation and session management
objectives: Test login forms for weak credential handling and predictable reset flows.
Check whether a user can reach functions that belong to another role.
Analyse session tokens for weakness, reuse and missing expiry.
Examine single sign on and token based login for common mistakes.
Verify that logout and password change really end the old session.

chapters.title: Injection and server side vulnerabilities
objectives: Test input fields for structured query language injection and confirm it safely.
Identify cross site scripting and choose the right proof of concept.
Check file upload and file path handling for unsafe behaviour.
Test for command injection and template injection where input reaches the system.
Explain how input validation and output encoding prevent these flaws.

chapters.title: Client side attacks
objectives: Explain how a browser decides what code may run on a page.
Test for cross site request forgery and describe the impact.
Identify cross site scripting flaws caused by unsafe document handling.
Assess clickjacking and other framing weaknesses.
Recommend browser side controls such as content security policy settings.

chapters.title: Application logic, other flaws and reporting
objectives: Test business rules by using workflows in an unexpected order.
Check for insecure direct references to files and records.
Review error handling and configuration for information leaks.
Rate each finding and write steps that reproduce it clearly.
Give developers a fix they can apply to the code or the design.
